'''''Rumex maritimus''''',  commonly called '''golden dock''', '''bristle dock''', or '''seashore dock''', is an annual plant species of the genus ''[[Rumex]]''. ''Rumex D maritimus'' grows in Argentina, Burma, Canada, China, and the United States. It is native to Canada and most of the 48 states.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=RUMA4|title=USDA Plants Database|last=|first=|date=|website=|access-date=}}</ref> The life span of ''Rumex maritimus'' is rarely biennial in moist environments.<ref name=":0" /> This herb belongs to the family Polygonaceae.

==Description  ==
''Rumex maritimus'' is composed of golden yellow or green/yellow [[inflorescence]]s on its leaves and stem. The plant ranges to be 15 cm to 75 cm high from the base of the plant.<ref name=":0" /> The stems of the plant grows upward or laying close to the ground with pedicels as long as 3 to 8 cm.  The leaves are wedged shaped, commonly narrow on both ends, but are rarely broadly wedded shaped. Its leaves range from 7 cm wide and 1.5 cm in height to 25 cm wide and 4 cm in height long containing blades that are [[lanceolate]] or lanceolate-linear.<ref name=":0" /> The flower of ''Rumex maritimus'' produces 15 to 30 triangular or rhombic triangular flowers ranging from 2.5 mm wide and .75 mm tall and 3mm wide to 1.2 mm tall.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242345752|title=Rumex maritimus in Flora of North America @ efloras.org|website=www.efloras.org|access-date=2019-10-03}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Rumex maritimus'' is very rare in [[Ireland]]<ref>Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora.'' Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref> but has been recorded from [[County Cork]], Ireland, from about 1870.<ref>Smiddy, P. 2016. Golden Dock (''Rumex maritimus'' L.: distribution and conservation problems in East Cork (H5), and records of an associate native species, Red Goosefoot (''Chaenophodium rubrum'' L.) Notes and records. ''Irish Naturalists' Journal'' '''35'''(1):52 - 54</ref> In Britain it is noted as local.<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968. ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles''. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|978-0521046565}}</ref> According to the U.S. federal government the Connecticut 'seaside dock' is in special concern for endangerment and in New York 'golden dock'  is endangered.<ref name=":0" /> Also according to the U.S. federal government ''Rumex'' is classified as a noxious weed.<ref name=":0" /> ''Rumex maritimus'' frequently grow in areas that flood with water. Shoots that are elongated are grown during mid summer or summer, while shoots that are not elongated reproduce during its flooding season because the water transports its seeds.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sman|first1=A. J. M. Van der|last2=Blom|first2=C. W. P. M.|last3=Barendse|first3=G. W. M.|date=1993|title=Flooding resistance and shoot elongation in relation to developmental stage and environmental conditions in Rumex maritimus L. and Rumex palustris Sm.|journal=New Phytologist|language=en|volume=125|issue=1|pages=73–84|doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.1993.tb03865.x|pmid=33874609|issn=1469-8137|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Uses ==
Most organs in ''Rumex maritimus'' are used for medical purposes. The seeds are used as sex stimulants, aphrodisiac. The leaves are used to cure external burns and ringworm. The roots of ''Rumex maritimus'' are used to cure skin diseases. ''Rumex maritimus'' is used for foods; for example, seeds are ground into powder and are used for porridge.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/288824346|title=Taxonomy and Traditional Medicine Practices of Polygonaceae (Smartweed) Family at Rajshahi, Bangladesh|last=Uddin|first=Kamal|date=|website=|access-date=}}</ref> The leaves are cooked as a vegetable.
